parentIntro: The Stage 2 bridge week — the same place-value pattern, one size up. Ten hundreds make a thousand, ten thousands make ten thousand. The diagnostic showed she already reads four-digit numbers, so this week is about the WHY: every step left is worth ten times more.
watchFor: Zeros inside big numbers are the trap — 3,047 gets read as “three hundred and forty seven”, and 10,600 gets written as 1000600. Say the columns out loud with her: “thousands, hundreds, tens, ones”. Also watch for guessing a digit's value from its look rather than its column.

demo.title: One step left, ten times bigger
demo.say: You already know hundreds, tens and ones. Today we add a new column — and the pattern just keeps going.

steps.caption: ten hundreds make one thousand
steps.say: If I stack ten hundred-squares, they make one big thousand block. Ten hundreds make one thousand.

steps.caption: 2 thousands, 6 hundreds = 2,600
steps.say: Two thousand blocks, and six hundred squares. Two thousand, six hundred.

steps.caption: 2 thousands, 6 hundreds, 1 ten, 3 ones
steps.say: Add one ten stick and three little ones. Two thousand, six hundred and thirteen.

steps.caption: the 6 is worth 600, the 2 is worth 2000
steps.say: Four digits, four jobs. The three is three ones, the one is one ten, the six is six hundred, and the two is two thousand. Every step to the left is ten times bigger!

weDo.problem: Build 4,208 — then say what each digit is worth.
weDo.model: Write the column headings on the whiteboard first: Th | H | T | O. Then write the digits underneath, one per column.
steps: Write the headings together, then read the number aloud slowly: “four thousand, two hundred and eight.”
Ask her to place each digit in its column. The empty tens column is the interesting one.
Ask: “What is the 4 worth?” (4000) “The 2?” (200) “What about the 0 — why is it there?” (To hold the tens column empty.)
Sneaky check: “what would this number be if I took the zero out?” (428 — a completely different number.)

weDo.model: A number line marked in thousands: 9,000 … 10,000 … 11,000. Mark 9,500 halfway along the first gap and jump.
steps: Ask her to find roughly where 9,500 sits (halfway between 9,000 and 10,000).
Jump forward one thousand and land. Ask what she's landed on.
If she says “ten thousand five hundred”, ask her to write it — this is where 10,500 vs 100500 gets tested.
Extend if she's flying: “what is 1,000 more than THAT?” (11,500)
